learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem in a Vue 3 application.

content.intro: This lesson studies Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem within Professional Practices, Legacy Projects, and Further Learning. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Production work continues after the first successful render: teams need a reproducible workflow for review, upgrades, bug reports, and releases.

content_blocks.title: Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem: Safe maintenance workflow
content_blocks.alt_text: Safe maintenance workflow diagram for lesson 150: Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem. Record versions, behavior, and constraints → Add a regression check before migration → Compare behavior and document recovery
content_blocks.caption: Maintenance flow: preserve existing behavior with inventory, incremental changes, repeatable checks, and a rollback plan.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. This lesson focuses on Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Vue CLI and its maintenance status
items.text: For Vue CLI and its maintenance status, inventory current behavior and dependency constraints before changing a legacy project. Make the smallest reversible change, add regression checks, and document why a new convention is safer or easier to maintain.

items.title: Migrating older projects to Vite
items.text: For Migrating older projects to Vite, trace the path from the entry point to the root component, then identify the configuration or tool responsible for compiling and serving it. Use the official create-vue/Vite workflow for a fresh Vue 3 project and keep dependency versions reproducible.

items.title: Understanding Vuex codebases
items.text: For Understanding Vuex codebases, define one source of truth and separate stored state from derived values and actions. Avoid duplicating the same fact in component-local state and a global store; persist only what the product genuinely needs.

items.title: Updating outdated patterns
items.text: For Updating outdated patterns, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

items.title: Evaluating third-party Vue libraries
items.text: For Evaluating third-party Vue libraries, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

content_blocks.code: Inventory runtime and dependencies → capture current behavior with tests → migrate one area → compare routes and interactions → document rollback.
content_blocks.expected_output: Migration is treated as a sequence of verifiable changes rather than an all-at-once rewrite.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use in a non-production branch with a lockfile and a written rollback plan. Vue 2 and Vue CLI are legacy-maintenance topics in this course.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Migrating older projects to Vite”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Professional Vue engineering covers maintainable code, version control, documentation, migration, shared UI systems, and responsible community work. For Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Legacy Tooling and Ecosystem” that applies “Vue CLI and its maintenance status”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Vue CLI and its maintenance status”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.
